newsitem.title: USA: Ford CEO Trotman's 1996 total compensation up 5.7 pct.
newsitem.headline: Ford CEO Trotman's 1996 total compensation up 5.7 pct.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Alex Trotman's total 1996 compensation grew 5.7 percent, despite lower bonuses for him and most of the automaker's other top executives.
Trotman's total compensation rose in 1996 to $5,738,976, thanks to his first base salary increase since taking over the automaker's top job, up from total compensation in 1995 of $5,431,354.
Ford made the figures available in its 1996 proxy statement, which was filed Monday. Ford was the first of the Big Three Detroit automakers to release its proxy.
The figures for both years do not include money he received from exercising stock options, or the present-day value of new options he was granted but has not exercised.

Of Trotman's total 1996 compensation, $3,669,551 is available to him now and $2,069,425 is deferred until after his retirement and is tied to the long-term performance of the company and the future value of Ford stock.
Ford said Trotman's base salary increased to $1,916,667 in 1996 from $1,500,000 in 1995, marking Trotman's first increase in base pay since he took over as Ford chairman in 1993.
But Trotman's bonus award fell 16.7 percent to $2.5 million in 1996 from $3 million in 1995.

Bonsuses also fell for Vice Chairmen Wayne Booker and Edward Hagenlocker, and Kenneth Whipple, president of the Ford's Financial Services Group. The only one to get a higher bonus was Jacques Nasser, the executive who has launched a massive cost-slashing crusade since becoming president of Ford's Automotive Operations in October.

Ford officials said Nasser, who got a bonus of $950,000 vs. $850,000 in 1995, received more money because of his promotion last year. He was previously in charge of the company's product development efforts.

Ford said bonuses overall were down because the board set aside less money to be awarded -- $169 million in 1996 vs. $192 million in 1995. The bonus pool is tied to Ford's performance and competitive data. If the amount of capital needed to run the business is up, as was the case in 1996, then the money used for bonuses falls, Ford officials said.

Ford's board of directors recently voted to extend Trotman's employment with the company until Jan. 1, 2000, delaying his retirement by about two years past age 65. Included in Trotman's $5.7 million total for 1996 is an award of restricted stock worth $700,429 that is generally available to him until 18 months after his retirement.

Not included in Trotman's 1996 compensation total is his exercising of stock options totaling $1,323,215. Also not included are new options to purchase 300,000 shares of Ford common stock at a price of $32.69 each. Ford estimated that those options have a present-day value of $2,079,000.
However, the option price is currently higher than Ford's stock price, which was up 75 cents on Monday to $31.625.

Ford also disclosed for the first time Monday that Trotman earned $1,260,000 in the form of restricted stock in 1995 under a long-term incentive payout. The payout for 1996 will not be determined until mid-1997, and will not be disclosed until Ford releases next year's proxy statement. The stock is restricted until after he retires.
